 Stereotact Funct Neurosurg 2010;88:183–186 
 DOI: 10.1 159/000313871 
 Spinal Cord Stimulation to Abort Painful 
Spasms of Atypical Stiff Limb Syndrome 
 I. Ughratdar    G. Sivakumar    S. Basu  
 Department of Neurosurgery, Queen’s Medical Centre,  Nottingham , UK

has not been documented in the English literature. We 
provide a brief overview of SLS and discuss the possible 
underlying mechanisms of the observed phenomenon.
  C a s e  R e p o r t  
 A 44-year-old man was referred to our unit for the revision of 
his spinal cord stimulator following hardware failure. He suffered 
a back injury 14 years ago and subsequently developed severe pain 
in his back and medial right thigh. This evolved into severe, pain-
ful, recurrent spasms of the whole right leg which were refractory 
to physiotherapy, non-steroidals, analgesics and epidural blocks.
  Electromyogram studies confirmed the failure to achieve elec-
trical silence in his right thoracolumbar paraspinal and right tib-
ialis posterior muscles in keeping with a diagnosis of SLS. This 
was labelled as atypical as he exhibited features of both SLS and 
stiff person syndrome (SPS), as well as testing negative for anti-
glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies. In 2004, follow-
ing a period of failed conservative management, he underwent a 
percutaneous implantation of a Medtronic /L50128  quadripolar SCS at 
level T 
10–11  which was connected to an implantable pulse genera-
tor (IPG). This device was successful in controlling the pain but he 
continued to experience debilitating spasms related to his SLS.
  He was referred to our unit in 2006 as his pain had returned. 
An interrogation of the SCS device revealed high impedance in 
all 4 contacts confirming hardware failure, and a revision was 
planned. The patient was severely debilitated by the return of his 
pain and also the progression of his spasms. The spasms occurred 
up to 4 times a day precipitated by minor knocks and would last 
between 1 and 4 h. He eventually developed chronic lymphoede-
ma of his right leg that resulted in a fixed inversion of the foot, 
confining him to his house. Pre-operatively his polypharmacy in-
cluded substantial doses of baclofen, benzodiazepines and vari-
ous opioid medications.
 Key Words 
 Spinal cord stimulation  /H11554  Stiff limb syndrome  /H11554  Spasms 
 Abstract 
 Stiff limb syndrome (SLS) is a rare chronic condition which 
can result in significant debility. We report the case of a 
44-year-old man suffering from severe painful spasms in his 
right leg with a diagnosis of SLS. He had been initially treated 
for his pain with a spinal cord stimulator but presented with 
exacerbation of pain secondary to a lead fracture for which 
he underwent revision of the stimulator. Postoperative pro-
gramming unexpectedly resulted in not only control of his 
pain but also an ability to abort his spasmodic episodes re-
lated to SLS. T o our knowledge, spinal cord stimulation has 
not been previously used for SLS and our report opens up 
another avenue for this rare condition. We provide a brief 
overview of SLS and propose an underlying mechanism for 
the observed phenomenon.

 Introduction 
 Spinal cord stimulation (SCS) has become an indis-
pensable tool in the armoury of the neurosurgeon to treat

chronic, refractory pain conditions. The knowledge of 
the mechanism of action, though fragmentary in nature, 
is related to the well-known gate-control theory for seg-
mental pain suppression. SCS has certainly been used to

  During the revision of the hardware it was noted that the pre-
viously implanted electrode had kinked suggesting an insulation 
break at the level of entry into the spine. The electrode was re-
placed at T 
10–11  with a Medtronic Resume TL and the extension 
wire was replaced and connected to the IPG. The stimulator was 
set with the following settings: pulse amplitude 3.0 V, range 0–5.0, 
pulse width 300  /H9262 s, pulse rate 60–130 Hz. As it was noted that the 
patient was only using the upper 2 contacts with the pre-revision 
stimulator, the replacement was positioned slightly more cepha-
lad, physiologically and radiologically midline.
  After the revision the SCS provided excellent coverage of the 
painful limb. During programming and whilst having a spas-
modic episode, it was unexpectedly noted that a high amplitude 
current with a wide pulse width could abort his spasms. The fol-
low-up 6 weeks later revealed that the patient was in fact using his 
stimulator to abort his spasmodic episodes more than for his pri-
mary indication of pain.
  At 1 year after the revision, his lymphoedema had completely 
resolved, the analgesia and benzodiazepine dependence had sig-
nificantly improved and more importantly his quality of life had 
improved. He was now able to mobilise with the use of 1 crutch 
and reach his local restaurant 150 yards away. He was also able to 
abort his spasm within 1 min of onset. He is due to see a pain spe-
cialist with a view to completely stopping all opiates.
  Discussion 
 SLS is a rare chronic relapsing remitting disorder af-
fecting one or both of the lower limbs. It presents with 
distal rigidity, stiffness and painful spasms of the lower 
limbs which may lead to abnormal posture. The spasms 
are spontaneous, reflex and induced by voluntary move-
ment or exteroceptive stimulation. They tend to affect the 
calf and foot, and this may result in difficulty with gait  
[1, 
2] . Most reported cases have isolated stiffness for several 
years, which in time progresses to involve the upper limbs 
leading to wheelchair dependence. Many cases eventu-
ally display mild sphincter or transient brain stem dys-
function but no evidence of long tract disturbance.
  The aetiology of the condition is poorly understood, 
with chronic spinal interneuronitis hypothesised as be-
ing the pathophysiology. Extensive investigations, in-
cluding neuroaxis imaging and immunological testing, 
have so far proved futile. Anti-GAD antibodies which are 
typically found in approximately 60% of SPS are usually 
absent. Electrophysiology usually features continuous 
motor unit activity present at rest in at least one limb 
muscle, with spasms involving repetitive grouped dis-
charge of motor units. Histologically, relatively selective 
destruction of spinal interneurones has been confirmed. 
Interestingly, the stimulus for spasms is not limited to 
somaesthetic stimulation below the level of the spinal 
c o r d  p a th o l o gy  wi th  r e p o rt e d  c a s e s  o f  s t a rtl e - i n d u c i n g  
stimuli including sounds. Presumably this represents an 
excessive response at the segmental level to descending 
reticulospinal activity  
[1] .
  Very few treatment modalities have been successful in 
this deb ili ta ting co n di ti o n. Bacl o f e n an d diazepam ha v e 
led to some reduction in the painful spasms. Other report-
ed treatment modalities have included intravenous immu-

noglobulin, plasmapheresis  
[3]  and intrathecal baclofen.
  The history of SCS for motor disorders has been recog-
nised since 1973 when Cook [see  4 ] published a paper on 
its use in multiple sclerosis. Since then, SCS has been ap-
plied to control a variety of motor disorders. Waltz et al.

[5]  reported a large series of patients in whom SCS was 
applied to control various disorders of the motor system. 
This group noted significant improvements in spasticity 
(94%) and athetosis (67%) associated with cerebral palsy. 
Painful spasms were also noted to be abolished or mark-
edly decreased in all patients. More modest improvement 
was recorded for the bladder, the balance and pseudobul-
bar symptoms. Patients with dystonic movements, spas-
modic torticollis and spasticity associated with post-
traumatic brain injury all showed significant improve-
ments in symptoms. Waltz et al. concluded that in 
carefully selected patients and careful individualisation 
with respect to level, polarity and frequency of stimula-
tion, good therapeutic results can be achieved in an eclec-
tic selection of motor disorders.
  In 1989, Cioni et al.  
[6]  studied the effects of SCS on 
motor performances in 11 patients with stabilised spastic 
hemiparesis secondary to cerebrovascular ischaemic ac-
cidents. They found an improvement in 7 out of 11 pa-
tients with neurophysiology confirming the deactivation 
of pathological patterns of voluntary movement with re-
duced agonist-antagonist co-activation and clonus. Inter-
estingly, they noticed that improvements with SCS only 
occurred in patients who had a sensory deficit. This led 
to the theory that the SCS enhanced sensory input, and 
as a consequence patients developed a new sensorimotor 
integration, i.e. the improvement may have been the re-
sult of a new relationship between ascending and de-
scending pathways.
  In 1995, Barolat et al.  
[7]  found a beneficial reduction 
in moderately intense spasms associated with traumatic 
and non-traumatic myelopathy that was refractory to 
medical treatment. Those patients with severe flexor 
spasms (with their knees almost up against the chest) did 
not benefit, and in these cases intrathecal baclofen was 
the preferred modality of treatment. No underlying 
mechanism was proposed in the study.

Spinal Cord Stimulation for Stiff Limb 
Syndrome 
Stereotact Funct Neurosurg 2010;88:183–186 185
  Despite sporadic reports  [5–8]  over the years of the 
beneficial effects of SCS on motor performance, the cur-
rent literature does not advocate motor performance as 
being an indication for its implantation. There have also 
been no such reports of patients suffering from SLS in 
whom an SCS was implanted successfully for painful 
spasms. Reasons for this may include the paucity of the 
condition and also the potential preference of surgeons to 
implant baclofen pumps in such patients. We report on 
the pathology of SLS and propose possible underlying 
mechanisms for the observed phenomenon in our case 
study.
  Functioning interneurones form an integral part of 
the control mechanisms ( fig. 1 ,  2 ) responsible for normal 
spinal cord ref lexes  
[9] . It is precisely these interneurones 
that are postulated to be affected in the disease process of 
SLS. Another proposed mechanism relates to GAD which 
is used by the body to convert glutamic acid to GABA, the 
inhibitory neurotransmitter. Anti-GAD antibodies are 
usually found in SPS and are absent in SLS, where it is 
postulated patients may have antibodies for post-synaptic 
elements like synaptophysin and GABA transaminase

[10] . With GABA production affected secondary to inter-
neurone damage both startle and central pattern genera-
tor systems are affected resulting in a cathartic discharge 
from the motor group.
  I n  o u r  r e p o r t  a  n u m b e r  o f  o b s e r v a t i o n s  w e r e  m a d e  
with respect to the abortion of the spasms:
  – The anti-spasmodic effect was only observed when the 
SCS was programmed to a higher current (ampere) 
with a wide pulse width (above 210 /H9262s). It is known 
that the physical effect of a wide pulse width and a high 
ampere current from a midline dorsally placed epidu-
ral electrode has greater and deeper recruitment of the 
spinal cord area in the current field. However, research 
has shown that in clinical situations the deeper and 
more ventral recruitment is unlikely to spread to the 
ventral motor tracts  
[11] .

 – The effect was rapid and cumulative but not instanta-
neous. The spasmodic episode was aborted as the 
spasm frequency and strength slowly decayed. In total 
it took approximately 80 s for the spasm to be aborted 
with the SCS, compared with the natural resolution 
time of anywhere between 1 and 4 h. This dramatic 
ability to arrest the spasm promptly has significantly 
improved the patient’s quality of life. 
 – No SCS-related aberrant motor activity was noted 
during up-programming of the ampere or afterwards. 
 – The patient did not feel any unpleasant sensation/pain 
when the higher current (ampere) was applied. In nor-
mal subjects high currents and wide pulse widths 
would probably produce unwanted effects. 
 – The anti-spasmodic effects outlasted the high current 
stimulation period such that post-stimulation and 
further exterostimulation did not provoke spasms. 
 – Switching off the stimulator brought about a return of 
the symptoms within a few hours suggesting that im-
provement of the symptoms with the SCS was not re-
lated to the natural history of the disease. 
 Naturally, the observations noted above have led us to 
extrapolate that the phenomenon is related to the theory 
for mechanism of action for SCS. We know that anti-
dromic conduction and modulation (gating) of sensory 
input to the dorsal horn has been a method of action for 
SCS  
[12] . Similarly, in SLS, at a high current, SCS can gate 
stretch reflex afferent input (1a and 1b fibres) at the dorsal 
horn and recruit inhibitory interneurones, thereby dis-
rupting a spasmodic episode and also preventing another 
one when the stimulation is on. To this effect, recent stud-
ies have confirmed that deep brain stimulation enhances 
intrinsic pathological activity at low frequencies, whereas 
at high frequencies it overrides it in the target nucleus and 
r e p l a c e s  t h i s  a c t i v i t y  w i t h  r e g u l a r i s e d  n e u r o n a l  f i r i n g

[13] .
  The regulation of dorsal horn transmitters and the 
neuromodulation effects of SCS have also been re-
searched. Specifically in neuropathic pain there is an in-
creased release of essential amino acids, which is in part 
due to a deficiency in local GABAergic function. One 
proposal is that SCS may induce an increased GABA re-
lease  
[14] , thereby suppressing the activity of essential 
amino acids possibly through activating the GABA B  re-
ceptor  [15] . Similar mechanisms may exist with the re-
lease of glycine, adenosine and 5-HT by SCS, probably 
originating from descending pathways, thus indicating 
an activation of supraspinal regions by SCS. The up-reg-
ulation in the availability of GABA in the spinal segments 
could explain the anti-spasmodic effect outlasting the 
stimulation.
  Conclusion 
 Though the mechanism is speculative, SCS may be-
come a useful adjunct in the management of intractable 
spasms associated with SLS. However, as this is the only 
case, further trials with careful selection and individu-
alisation of the stimulation parameters are indicated.
